title: 2 Samuel 18:9–18
context: Absalom is caught by his head in an oak. A soldier refuses to harm him because of the king’s order, but Joab kills him, and his armor-bearers finish the act. Absalom is buried under a heap of stones in the forest, and the narrator recalls the pillar he set up for himself because he had no son to carry his name.

verses.text: Absalom happened to meet David’s servants. Absalom was riding on his mule, and the mule went under the thick boughs of a great oak; and his head caught hold of the oak, and he was hanging between the sky and earth; and the mule that was under him went on.
verses.arminianNotes: Absalom’s head catches in the boughs of a great oak, and his mule goes on without him. Arminian readers note the sudden reversal of a man who had freely pursued glory and the throne, now helpless between sky and earth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s purpose from 17:14 coming to its end in an unexpected way. A popular tradition links the scene to Absalom’s famous hair (14:26), but the text says only that his head was caught, and readers should not press beyond it.

verses.text: A certain man saw it, and told Joab, and said, “Behold, I saw Absalom hanging in an oak.”
verses.arminianNotes: A soldier sees Absalom hanging and reports it to Joab rather than acting himself. Arminian readers note this man’s free and conscientious choice to respect the king’s order even when he could have struck.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the scene setting up a contrast between an ordinary soldier who honors the king’s word and a powerful commander who will not. Obedience is tested in the small moments.

verses.text: Joab said to the man who told him, “Behold, you saw it, and why didn’t you strike him there to the ground? I would have given you ten pieces of silver and a sash.”
verses.arminianNotes: Joab rebukes the man for not striking Absalom and mentions the reward he would have paid. Arminian readers see Joab weighing political advantage over the king’s explicit command, a choice he is responsible for.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Joab offers silver and a sash to tempt obedience away from the king. His willingness to buy disobedience reveals a pragmatism that runs through his career.

verses.text: The man said to Joab, “Though I should receive a thousand pieces of silver in my hand, I still wouldn’t stretch out my hand against the king’s son; for in our hearing the king commanded you and Abishai and Ittai, saying, ‘Beware that no one touch the young man Absalom.’
verses.arminianNotes: The soldier says that even a thousand pieces of silver would not make him harm the king’s son, because all heard David’s order. Arminian readers admire his integrity, freely refusing a bribe for the sake of conscience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the soldier a picture of faithful submission to lawful authority. He quotes the king’s command exactly, showing that he took David’s word seriously.

verses.text: Otherwise, if I had dealt falsely against his life (and there is no matter hidden from the king), then you yourself would have set yourself against me.”
verses.arminianNotes: The soldier adds that nothing is hidden from the king, and Joab would have turned against him. Arminian readers note his clear-eyed realism about Joab’s character as well as his loyalty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe the soldier’s prudence: he knows that disobedience would come to light. His words also expose the self-serving way Joab treats those under him.

verses.text: Then Joab said, “I’m not going to wait like this with you.” He took three darts in his hand and thrust them through Absalom’s heart while he was still alive in the middle of the oak.
verses.arminianNotes: Joab refuses to wait, takes three darts, and thrusts them into Absalom while he is still alive in the oak. Arminian readers see a deliberate decision to override the king’s order, judging that Absalom’s death served the kingdom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God’s purpose to bring evil on Absalom (17:14) is fulfilled, yet Joab remains accountable for disobeying David. David later charges Solomon concerning Joab’s violence (1 Kings 2:5-6).

verses.text: Ten young men who bore Joab’s armor surrounded and struck Absalom, and killed him.
verses.arminianNotes: Ten young armor-bearers surround Absalom and finish the killing. Arminian readers note the collective act, which spreads responsibility but does not erase it. Each one chose to take part.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe the narrator’s restraint, recording the death briefly and without relish. The rebellion ends, but the manner of it will grieve the king.

verses.text: Joab blew the trumpet, and the people returned from pursuing after Israel; for Joab held the people back.
verses.arminianNotes: Joab blows the trumpet and holds the people back from further pursuit. Arminian readers see a commander who, having secured his aim, restrains needless bloodshed among fellow Israelites.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that with Absalom dead the rebellion has lost its head, so continued slaughter would only deepen division within Israel. Joab’s order limits the cost of civil war.

verses.text: They took Absalom and cast him into a great pit in the forest, and raised over him a very great heap of stones. Then all Israel fled, each to his own tent.
verses.arminianNotes: Absalom is thrown into a pit in the forest and covered with a great heap of stones, and Israel scatters. Arminian readers note the dishonorable burial for one who had sought the honor of a king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers often compare the heap of stones with those raised over Achan (Joshua 7:26) and the king of Ai (Joshua 8:29). Such burials marked judgment, a sobering end to rebellion.

verses.text: Now Absalom in his lifetime had taken and reared up for himself the pillar which is in the king’s valley, for he said, “I have no son to keep my name in memory.” He called the pillar after his own name. It is called Absalom’s monument, to this day.
verses.arminianNotes: Absalom had set up a pillar in the king’s valley because he said he had no son to keep his name. Arminian readers note the contrast between the monument he raised for himself and the shameful pit where he lies.
verses.reformedNotes: Second Samuel 14:27 says Absalom had three sons, so interpreters often suggest they died young or that the pillar predates their birth; the text does not say. Reformed readers see the futility of seeking a lasting name apart from God.
